Exposure-response estimate with a bootstrap sensitivity interval

Source: R/aexp.R
exprspplr.Rd

Fits the partially linear exposure-response model (the effect of an exposure on an outcome, the confounders partialled out by cross-fitted regressions), or any estimator with the same interface, then re-fits it on nboot non-parametric resamples of the rows for a percentile interval (Efron and Tibshirani 1993, chapter 13). The bootstrap interval does not lean on the estimator's own standard error, so it is a check on it: when the two disagree, the analytic one should not be trusted alone.

Usage

exprspplr(data, y, expo, confs, nboot = 100L, rstate = 42L, estr = NULL)

# S3 method for class 'exprspplr'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

data

A data frame, one row per unit (an area and period, a person).

y, expo, confs

Column names: the outcome and the exposure (single strings) and the confounders (one or more strings).

nboot

Number of resamples, a non-negative whole number (default 100); at least 10 must succeed.

rstate

Seed for the resampling (default 42), a whole number from -2147483647 to \(2^{53} - 1\).

estr

NULL (the default) for the built-in cross-fitted partially linear regression, or a function (or the name of one) (data, outcome, treatment, covariates) returning a list with ate and se (and optionally method).

x

A result of exprspplr().

...

Not used.

Value

A list of class exprspplr with ate (the full-sample estimate), seana (the estimator's standard error), seboot (the standard deviation of the replicates), cilobs and ciupbs (the 95\ number of successful resamples) and method (the estimator's method with " + percentile bootstrap").

Details

In environmental criminology the exposure is a pollutant or heat and the outcome a count of offences or victimisations by place and period, with the neighbourhood's population and deprivation as confounders: the estimate is the change in the outcome per unit of exposure.

The built-in estimator (estr = NULL) is the partially linear regression \(y = \theta d + g(x) + e\) fitted by double machine learning with cross-fitting (the DML2 estimator of Chernozhukov et al. 2018): the rows with every column present are split at random into five folds, the outcome and the exposure are each regressed on the confounders by ordinary least squares on four folds and predicted on the fifth, and \(\theta\) is the regression of the outcome's residuals on the exposure's, with the heteroskedasticity-robust standard error. The folds are drawn from R's generator seeded with 1 for every fit, the stream then restored, so the estimate does not depend on the session. It refuses a column that is not numeric, fewer than ten complete rows, and an exposure with no variation left after the confounders are partialled out.

Each resample draws nrow(data) rows with replacement and calls estr(resample, y, expo, confs); a resample on which the estimator fails is skipped, and the run stops if fewer than 10 succeed. The interval is the 2.5\ seboot their standard deviation. Resampling uses R's generator seeded with rstate and restores R's own random stream afterwards. The cost is nboot + 1 estimator calls; the built-in estimator runs in the compiled core.

Refusals: column names that are not strings, an nboot that is not a single non-negative whole number, an estimator that is not a function, and the estimator's own errors on the full sample.

References

Efron, B. and Tibshirani, R. J. (1993). An Introduction to the Bootstrap. Chapman and Hall.

Chernozhukov, V., Chetverikov, D., Demirer, M., Duflo, E., Hansen, C., Newey, W. and Robins, J. (2018). Double/debiased machine learning for treatment and structural parameters. The Econometrics Journal 21(1), C1-C68. doi:10.1111/ectj.12097

See also

dmlx for double machine learning with other learners and models.

Examples

# simulated areas: exposure driven by x1, the outcome by the exposure and
# x2
set.seed(1)
d <- data.frame(x1 = rnorm(200), x2 = rnorm(200))
d$exposure <- 20 + 2 * d$x1 + rnorm(200)
d$asthma <- 5 + 0.3 * d$exposure + d$x2 + rnorm(200)
r <- exprspplr(d, y = "asthma", expo = "exposure", confs = c("x1", "x2"),
               nboot = 20)
r$ate
#> [1] 0.2536464
c(r$cilobs, r$ciupbs)
#> [1] 0.1365177 0.3476568

# Any estimator with the same interface: here an ordinary regression.
ols <- function(data, outcome, treatment, covariates) {
  f <- stats::reformulate(c(treatment, covariates), outcome)
  cf <- summary(stats::lm(f, data = data))$coefficients
  list(ate = cf[treatment, 1], se = cf[treatment, 2], method = "OLS")
}
exprspplr(d, "asthma", "exposure", c("x1", "x2"), nboot = 20,
          estr = ols)$method
#> [1] "OLS + percentile bootstrap"

# Fewer than 10 resamples cannot give an interval.
try(exprspplr(d, "asthma", "exposure", c("x1", "x2"), nboot = 5))
#> Error : exprspplr: Only 5 successful bootstrap fits; need >=10. Inspect the model's convergence on your resamples.
